title: Policy Gambit: Routing Playbook for Latency-Cost-Reliability Tradeoffs
content:
Purpose and context:

This is a working playbook for a policy-first routing layer that balances latency, cost, and reliability across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. It collects heuristics, a lightweight decision-tree template, scoring primitives, and operational test cases we can iterate on in the control plane. Goal is to produce a policy DSL + defaults that engineers can adopt without deep infra knowledge but that platform teams can tune for high-value customers.

Why a different angle (the ‘gambit’):
- Most docs define optimizers or scorecards. This doc frames the problem as a set of routing gambits (policy moves) with clear probes and rollbacks — easier to teach to SREs and product engineers.
- Emphasizes small, verifiable policy primitives plus a human-reviewable decision tree per customer/route.

High-level requirements (derived):
- Latency SLOs: p95/p99 targets per route; soft vs hard SLOs for different tiers.
- Cost sensitivity: route-level cost-per-token budget or weighted preference (e.g., 0.6 latency / 0.4 cost).
- Reliability guardrails: minimum success rate, regional redundancy, automatic fallback to lower-capacity models when nodes fail.
- Observability: token-level cost trace, route-level latency histograms, fail-rate alarms tied to policy triggers.

Primitive signals (inputs to policies):
- liveLatencyMs: short-window (30s) p50/p95/p99 by region/model variant.
- queueDepth: number of pending requests at serving pool.
- tokenCostPerSec: aggregated cost burn rate (estimate).
- errorRate: 5xx + model-failure-rate rolling 5m/1h.
- capacityScore: normalized available GPU cycles (0..1) per pool.
- userPriority: customer tier (free, pro, enterprise).
- routeCriticality: application-level (edge search vs background embedding).

Scoring primitives and utility function (suggested):
- Normalize signals to 0..1 (0 best for latency/cost/error depending on orientation). Use sigmoid smoothing near thresholds to avoid flapping.
- latencyScore = clip((p95 - target) / target, -1, 3) mapped into 0..1 via logistic: latencyScoreNorm = 1/(1+exp(-k * latencyScore))
- costScore = scaled currentCost / budget => costScoreNorm = min(1, currentCost/budget)
- reliabilityScore = 1 - successRate (higher is worse); reliabilityNorm = reliabilityScore (already 0..1)
- compositeUtility = w_latency * (1 - latencyScoreNorm) + w_cost * (1 - costScoreNorm) + w_reliability * (1 - reliabilityNorm)

Notes: We expose weights (w_latency, w_cost, w_reliability) at policy level. Default for interactive routes: {0.6, 0.2, 0.2}. For batch/embeddings: {0.2, 0.7, 0.1}.

Decision-tree template (human-readable first, then pseudo):
- Leaf nodes are actions: route_to(primary_pool), route_to(fallback_pool), degrade_model(quantized_variant), throttle(client_id, rate), fail_open(serve-best-effort), do_not_route(error).
- Internal nodes are checks: if latency.p95 > X then ... elif cost.burn > Y then ... else ...

Example tree for an interactive route (sketch):
1) If reliabilityNorm > 0.1 (i.e., errorRate > 10%) -> action: immediate fallback to regional replica in different region or to lower-tier model in same region; fire high-severity alert; increment incident counter for route.
2) Else if latency.p95 > latency_target * 1.5 and capacityScore < 0.3 -> action: route 30% of traffic to low-cost fallback + enable opportunistic batching; set short TTL cache for prefixes.
3) Else if cost burn rate exceeds budget for this window and userPriority == free -> action: switch to quantized model variant + throttle concurrency per key.
4) Else -> route_to(primary_pool)

Pseudo policy DSL example (compact):
policy "interactive-1" {
  weights { latency:0.6 cost:0.2 reliability:0.2 }
  targets { latency.p95: 200 } // ms
  budget { window_mins: 60, tokens: 3_000_000 }

  when reliability.errorRate_5m > 0.1 {
    action { fallback: regional-replica, alert: high }
  }

  when latency.p95 > 1.5 * targets.latency.p95 and capacityScore < 0.3 {
    action { split: { primary:70, fallback-quant:30 }, enable: batching(50ms) }
  }

  when budget.window_burn > 0.8 and userPriority == "free" {
    action { degrade: quant8, throttle: client_qps=1 }
  }

  default { route: primary_pool }
}

Edge cases and heuristics to avoid oscillation:
- Add minimum action duration (e.g., 30s) and cooldown windows equal to policy evaluation window. Do not flip actions faster than cooldown.
- Use EWMA of signals with two time constants: short (30s) for responsiveness, long (10m) for stability. Only trigger policy changes when both short and long indicate degradation beyond thresholds (helps avoid blips).
- Add hysteresis: different thresholds for entering/exiting the same branch (enter at 1.5x, exit at 1.2x).

Testing and validation playbook (stage -> prod):
- Unit tests: policy interpreter runs on synthetic signal traces (we keep a small test corpus of “gold” traces for p95 spikes, cascading failures, network partition). Each policy must pass expected-action assertions.
- Integration in sandbox region: deploy policy with dry-run flag (generate planned actions without taking them) for 24–72h and compare planned vs desired.
- Canary: rollout 5% traffic with enforced actions and close monitoring. If utility delta negative beyond threshold for 10m -> rollback.
- Chaos test: introduce synthetic error bursts and capacity pressure in staging to ensure fallback logic and degrade_model path work end-to-end.

Operational runbooks (quick):
- If P95 spikes in region A only: check capacityScore and queueDepth; if both elevated and reliability OK -> increase local pool autoscale or reroute limited traffic to region B.
- If errorRate across many models rises > 5%: switch to stable model variant (pinned) and open investigation.
- If cost burn exceeds scheduled commitment: enable cost-protect mode that reduces concurrency for free tier and routes heavy customers to dedicated pools (requires integration with billing signals).

Policy metrics we must emit per decision: 
- policy_eval_id, policy_version, decision_taken, decision_confidence (compositeUtility), signals_used (list), affected_fraction, time_window, actor (auto/manual).
These must be queryable in Console and included in trace for specific request IDs when decisions were applied.

Example decision trace (text):
- 2024-11-12T04:33Z policy_eval_id=pe-00412 policy=interactive-1 v=2 action=split(primary:70,fallback-quant:30) reasons=[latency.p95=420>target(200)*1.5, capacityScore=0.2] confidence=0.68 affected_fraction=0.3

Open questions / suggested experiments (for next sprint):
1) Can we learn weights (w_latency/cost/reliability) per-route from business signals (user retention or revenue impact) via offline bandit-style optimization?
2) Evaluate cost of batching vs latency per model family (Llama-like vs MPT-like) — build microbenchmarks and expose per-model batching sweet spot.
3) Tight integration with billing stream to provide real-time budget enforcement at route-level without huge processing lag.
4) Evaluate per-customer custom policies vs org-wide defaults — what is the minimum set of knobs to expose in self-serve?

Rollout checklist (MVP):
- [ ] Implement policy DSL parser + stable interpreter with test harness
- [ ] Emit decision telemetry with request-level linkage
- [ ] Implement cooldown/hysteresis primitives and EWMA signal windows
- [ ] Add policy dry-run mode and console visualization (planned vs executed)
- [ ] Run 2 chaos experiments in staging to verify fallback behavior

Notes to reviewers:
- This file is intentionally prescriptive in small steps; I expect the team to push back on specific numeric defaults. Please add concrete test traces if you have tough customer scenarios.
- Attached analytics queries and a short notebook will follow that simulates the compositeUtility under sample traces.

Appendix: quick cheat heuristics (copyable bullets)
- Prefer regional routing for latency unless capacityScore < 0.25 or errorRate > 0.05.
- If cost budget hits 70% and userPriority == free -> consider quantize + throttle; if enterprise -> prefer burst-to-dedicated or notify sales.
- For multi-region reads: prefer cross-region fallback only if inter-region latency < 80ms to avoid user-perceived lag.
